roediger2006.label: Roediger & Karpicke (2006). Test-enhanced learning. Psychological Science, 17(3), 249–255.

dunlosky2013.label: Dunlosky et al. (2013). Improving students’ learning with effective learning techniques. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 14(1), 4–58.

cepeda2006.label: Cepeda et al. (2006). Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(3), 354–380.

rohrer2007.label: Rohrer & Taylor (2007). The shuffling of mathematics problems improves learning. Instructional Science, 35(6), 481–498.

bjork1994.label: Bjork (1994). Memory and metamemory considerations in the training of human beings. In Metcalfe & Shimamura (Eds.), Metacognition: Knowing about knowing, 185–205. MIT Press.

koriat2005.label: Koriat & Bjork (2005). Illusions of competence in monitoring one’s knowledge during study. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 31(2), 187–194.

butler2008.label: Butler & Roediger (2008). Feedback enhances the positive effects and reduces the negative effects of multiple-choice testing. Memory & Cognition, 36(3), 604–616.

kornell2009.label: Kornell (2009). Optimising learning using flashcards: Spacing is more effective than cramming. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 23(9), 1297–1317.

rawson2011.label: Rawson & Dunlosky (2011). Optimizing schedules of retrieval practice for durable and efficient learning: How much is enough? Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 140(3), 283–302.

options.label: Rereading your notes until they feel familiar
Recalling information from memory, for example answering questions without looking
Highlighting the key sentences in a chapter
Copying a summary out again more neatly

items.explanation: Retrieval practice means pulling information out of memory, such as self-testing. Recalling strengthens later recall more than rereading the same material.

options.label: Leaving blank space in your notes helps you remember them
Breaks during a session make no difference to memory
Spreading study over separate sessions leads to better long-term memory than one massed session
Studying in a different room each time always improves recall

items.explanation: The same total study time, spread across separate sessions, produces better retention later than massing it into one session.

options.label: Studying one topic until you have mastered it before starting the next
Alternating study with exercise
Reading two textbooks side by side
Mixing different topics or problem types within one study session

items.explanation: Interleaving mixes problem types in one session, so you practise choosing the right method as well as applying it.

items.prompt: Why does spaced study tend to beat one long session of the same total length?

options.label: The brain can store only a fixed number of facts per day
Some forgetting between sessions makes the next recall more effortful, and that effort strengthens memory
Spaced sessions let you skip the hardest material
Long sessions always end up shorter than planned

items.explanation: One leading account: a gap lets some forgetting happen, so the next session takes more effort to recall, and that ‘desirable difficulty’ makes learning last.

items.prompt: Rereading a chapter three times makes it feel familiar. Why is that feeling a poor guide to what you will recall in the exam?

options.label: Recognising material while it is in front of you is not the same as recalling it without it
Rereading erases what you learned earlier
Familiar material is never tested
The feeling is accurate; rereading is the best method

items.explanation: Judging what you know while the answer is in view overestimates what you can recall later, when it is not.

items.prompt: Exam questions come in a mixed order. Why does practising mixed problem types help with that?

options.label: It makes each practice session shorter
It lets you leave out the hardest problem types
It trains you to decide which method a problem needs, not only to apply a method you were told to use
It only works for learning languages

items.explanation: Blocked practice tells you the method in advance. Mixed practice makes you choose it, which is what a mixed exam asks for.

items.prompt: Your mock exam is in 6 days. You can study 2 hours a day, and it covers three topics. What do you do today?

options.label: Spend both hours rereading topic 1
Wait until the last two days so it is fresh
Make highlighted summaries of all three topics
Study each topic briefly, end with a short self-test on each, and plan to come back to all three on later days

items.explanation: This plan combines retrieval practice, spacing and mixing topics, the techniques rated most useful in a large review.

items.prompt: You finish a practice set and get 6 of 10 right. What is the most useful next move?

options.label: Check the right answers for the 4 you missed, then try those questions again from memory a few days later
Move on: 6 of 10 is a pass
Reread the whole chapter from the start
Repeat the same 10 questions straight away until you get 10 of 10

items.explanation: Feedback after a test corrects errors, and retrying after a gap turns the fix into durable learning; instant repeats mostly measure short-term memory.

items.prompt: You have 40 flashcards to learn over a week. Which approach fits the evidence best?

options.label: Split them into 4 piles of 10 and master one pile per sitting
Keep all 40 in one deck, cycle through it over several days, and recall each answer before you flip
Read the front and back together to save time
Drop a card as soon as you get it right once

items.explanation: One large deck spaces the repetitions of each card further apart, which beat small, crammed piles in a flashcard study.

items.prompt: A learner’s log: on day 1, after rereading a chapter four times in a row, they score 90% on a practice quiz. On day 7 they score 45% on a test of the same chapter. What best explains the drop?

options.label: The day 7 test was unfair
Four rereads were too few; eight would have fixed it
Massed rereading lifted the immediate score but did not last; spaced retrieval would have made it more durable
Memory always halves after a week, whatever the method

items.explanation: In a classic study, rereading did better on a test after 5 minutes, but self-testing did better a week later. Immediate scores can mislead.

items.prompt: Two students study for the same 3 hours. A studies 1 hour on Monday, Wednesday and Friday, ending each session with a self-quiz. B studies 3 hours on Friday, rereading notes. On Friday evening they score the same. What is the best prediction for a test the following Friday?

options.label: They will score the same again
B will score higher, because the material was fresher
It cannot be predicted from study methods
A will probably score higher, because spaced retrieval slows forgetting

items.explanation: Equal scores soon after study can hide different rates of forgetting. In a classic study, rereading did better on a test 5 minutes later, but self-testing did better a week later.

items.prompt: A class practises four problem types. Group 1 practises them in blocks (all of type A, then all of type B, and so on); Group 2 practises them shuffled. Group 1 scores higher during practice, but Group 2 scores higher on a later mixed test. What explains the reversal?

options.label: Blocked practice gives the method away, which lifts practice scores but not the skill of choosing a method that a mixed test needs
Group 2 got easier problems
Group 1 practised too much and forgot
Shuffled practice includes more problems

items.explanation: This pattern, worse during practice and better on the later test, is what interleaving studies with maths problems found.

items.prompt: An exam is in 2 weeks and you have 8 hours. Plan A: eight 1-hour sessions spread over the two weeks, each starting with a self-test on earlier material. Plan B: two 4-hour sessions on the final weekend, rereading and highlighting.

options.label: Plan A
Plan B
They are about equal
It uses more total time
It combines spacing with retrieval practice
Highlighting finds the key ideas quickly
Studying close to the exam keeps it fresh

items.explanation: Both plans use 8 hours. Plan A spreads them out and tests memory each time; rereading and highlighting rate low in the evidence.

items.prompt: A study app says: “Our learners feel 30% more confident after one session of rereading our summaries.”

parts.prompt: Is that good evidence that the method works?

options.label: Yes
No
Confidence after rereading often reflects familiarity, not what you can recall later
Confidence cannot be measured
30% is too small to matter

items.explanation: Confidence during study often overestimates later recall, because familiar material feels known. The claim needs a test of recall days later.

items.prompt: A tutor advises: “Only use practice tests at the end, once you have learned everything. Testing too early just shows you what you don’t know.”

options.label: Sound
Unsound
Testing is itself a learning event, and it helps throughout study, especially with feedback
Tests are only useful for grading
Early tests always lower motivation

items.explanation: A large review rated practice testing among the most useful study techniques, used throughout study rather than saved for the end. Low-stakes tests help you learn, not only measure what you know.

items.prompt: Your mock exam covers topics A, B and C. Put these 8 study blocks in the order you would do them over the week before the mock.

options.label: Topic A: learn
Topic A: self-test
Topic B: learn
Topic B: self-test
Topic C: learn
Topic C: self-test
Mock exam
Mixed self-test on A, B and C

items.explanation: A plan that works: learn each topic, come back to test it after a gap, and take the mixed self-test after all the topic tests. Mixing topics in one session (interleaving) helps you tell them apart (Rohrer & Taylor, 2007).
items.notCorrectFeedback: This plan doesn't build in spacing yet

items.prompt: Put the steps of one self-testing session in order.

options.label: Check your answers against the source
Plan when to retry the ones you missed, in a few days
Write down everything you remember about the topic
Mark the questions you missed
Close the book and your notes
Answer practice questions without looking

items.explanation: Recall first with nothing in view, then check against the source for feedback, and schedule a delayed retry of what you missed.

items.prompt: Your exam mixes four kinds of volume problem. Arrange these 8 practice problems into one session that prepares you for it.

options.label: Cylinder volume, problem 1
Cylinder volume, problem 2
Cone volume, problem 1
Cone volume, problem 2
Sphere volume, problem 1
Sphere volume, problem 2
Prism volume, problem 1
Prism volume, problem 2

items.explanation: No two problems of the same kind back to back: each problem makes you work out which formula it needs, as the exam will.

novice.title: Turn one chapter into 10 questions and answer them from memory
Explain in your own words why recalling beats rereading
Spread one topic over three short sessions this week

advanced_beginner.title: Plan a week that spaces each topic across at least two days
Mix two topics in one practice set
Compare your score after a 3-day gap with your same-day score

competent.title: Find your weakest topic from your practice-test log
Rate two revision plans against spacing and retrieval
Adjust next week’s schedule after each self-test

proficient.title: Design a 4-week revision plan with growing gaps between reviews
Judge a study app’s claims against the evidence
Coach a classmate through one retrieval session

expert.title: Design a revision plan for a subject you have not studied before
Build a question bank someone else can revise from
